units.translation: and in these adornments, greatly mocked by friends
Why then do I have this mockery of myself?
so that justice may be rightly decided
In which sense it is frequently said of exiles: see Thes. vol. 4 p. 1050.
I will bring back this man
if the gold-wrought letters bring him back
and Justice brought him back after he had been raised
and we will bury him not with lamentations

A word very common among the tragedians, who use only two tenses, the aorist κατθανείν [to die] and the future κατθανεῖσθαι [to be about to die], and these only with syncope admitted: for this very reason they are found not to have used the aorist indicative except where it was permitted to omit the augment, as in the anapaestic verse Ag. 1553 πρὸς ἡμῶν κάππεσε κάτθανε [by our hands he fell and died].
whom not even in death does the earth conceal
you say that the sea-drenched bodies of the dead are carried
once for each, having died in a shape
but to die gloriously is a grace for a mortal
so beautiful indeed is death to me
by our hands he fell and died

It is an epithet of Jupiter the thunderer, who is always called thus, never καταβάτης [descender]: on which see Thes. vol. 4 p. 1025. Hence καταιβάτης κεραυνός [descending thunderbolt] is a falling thunderbolt in Aeschylus Pr. 359 and others indicated in Thes.
before the blasts of Ares rush upon
and I will burn up the house of Amphion

What is read in Plut. Mor. p. 827 c is suspect: ἀναγκαζόμενον τὸ Αἰσχύλειον [being compelled to utter the Aeschylean line] (fr.302) ἀναφωνεῖν, ᾧ πρὸς τὴν τύχην ἐχρῆτο Δημήτριος ὁ πολιορκητὴς ἀποβαλὼν τὴν ηγεμονίαν [to cry out, which Demetrius the Besieger used to address to fortune after losing his command] “σύ του με φυσᾷς, σύ με καταίθειν δοκεῖς [you indeed beget me, you seem to burn me]. The same in V. Demetrii c. 35 p. 9054: διὸ καί φασιν αὐτὸν ἐν ταῖς χείροσι μεταβολαῖς πρὸς τὴν τύχην ἀναφθέγγεσθαι τὸ Αἰσχύλειον [therefore they say that in his worst reversals he uttered to fortune the Aeschylean line] “σύ τοί μ᾿ ἔφυσας [you indeed begot me] (other books have με φυσάς [you beget me], as written in Plut. Mor.), σύ με καταίθειν δοκεῖς [you seem to burn me]. On the last words Sintenis noted these variants of the books: "σύ με καταίθειν δοκεῖς [you seem to burn me] P. D. and Moral. 1. c. σύ μοι καταίθειν δοκεῖς [you seem to burn for me] B. C. and it had been in A, but corrected to σύ με καταίθειν δοκεῖς [you seem to burn me]. Commonly σύ με καταίθειν μοι δοκεῖς [you seem to me to burn me], which is in cod. 1679." Grotius' conjecture σύ τοί μ᾿ ἔφυσας, σύ με καταφθιεῖν δοκεῖς [you indeed begot me, you seem to destroy me] provides a fitting sense, except that he should have written καταφθίσειν [to be about to destroy].
burning (thus Canterus for κ ' αἴθουσα) the bloody torch of her child, of the same age
being compelled to utter the Aeschylean line
to cry out, which Demetrius the Besieger used to address to fortune after losing his command: "you indeed beget me, you seem to burn me"
therefore they say that in his worst reversals he uttered to fortune the Aeschylean line: "you indeed begot me"
